units.tr: I will not open the sanctuary of your merits. You were above all the author of my writing after the books of Augustus, and you did not let my leisure be buried in forgetfulness. At your urging, Europe was published in verse; at your urging, the secrets of kingdoms hiding among the adversaries came forth to be seen by the world. You, having shared the matter with the illustrious house of Nassau, gave me the opportunity to take up the task of writing the history of that family, among the most ancient of the German nobles, from its cradle to this age, and the deeds done in the Low Countries by the sword and by counsel from the beginning of the upheavals. As for the main point of this cause: since you often asked me for an account of the ancient writers, and since no more convenient crop presents itself now, owing to the need to defer the inaugural lecture, I have touched this paper without labouring over it. So, as they say, by one leap I have hunted two hares: I have fulfilled the duty laid on me by academic custom and satisfied your wish. I have avoided debt, and I pay what I can from my slender means, however little that is. I neither consulted nor had at hand the judgments of others on which authors are to be read. In this very list of readings I have relied on my memory rather than on the abundance of the library, and I ask pardon for that. I shall obtain it more easily if I have passed over anyone in that vast crowd of writers. Accept therefore, most learned sir, either the payment of a debt or a payment made in advance of one, perhaps to be recovered with greater interest once you have more leisure. But if the men of your Nassau and your country do not dislike these things, I do not fear the censure of the senate of the lesser nations. Given at Marburg, in the land of the Chatti, on the Ides of October, in the year of Christ 1656.

units.tr: When I cast myself into this gathering of select nobility, and reflect on the necessity of speaking imposed by academic custom, a certain trembling of mind arises, struggling between confidence and flight. I am a man of slender talent and of very little eloquence. The things that help even firm orators to deliver a full speech are a steady confidence of mind and a familiar sight of the listeners. Of these, the first my natural disposition long ago withdrew from me, and the second the unfamiliar appearance of this theatre now takes away. Even if all these were present, exactly as I would wish, the lack of things to say and the crowd of things to say would both pour over my mind. The poverty of expression and the hesitation of mind in searching the wood (of material)

units.la: nem, gignit praecepta tot statibus ma- teria, & totin pulpitis decantata can- tio. units.tr: are begotten by a subject that has been taught in so many places and sung in so many pulpits. Who would listen calmly to a discourse on the highest good or some virtue? Who would hold forth on the dignity of philosophy, which is set over the regulation of morals? Not to mention the envy stirred by a comparison with another's profession, and the hatred aroused by an encomium of the profession I have taken up. Not to mention praising a thing that does not need praise, and commending itself as if for hire. For who is so far from common sense, who so ignorant of literary care, as to stain with hatred or contempt that part of human wisdom which tames the passions, which exult wantonly above the ruling mind, and which governs cities, nations and peoples? I complain of the narrowness of my subject and the thinness of what I have to say. Yet a crop, ample in its yield and ripe for the harvest, has been thrown before my mind beyond my expectation, and compels it to turn to the opposite thought. When I look at the fertility of so wide a field, and consider the faculty of speaking with order and elegance, to be adapted to the senses of the listeners, I feel that I am stuck in the starting-gates, the goal not yet in view. But since one must obey the mistress of necessity, and submit to the rule of custom, no one would be so unfair a judge of the audience as not to excuse my boldness and presumption, or relieve my weakness, by the same guides that drive me: necessity, I say, and custom.

units.la: Quicquid cognitionis humanæ, imi subsellii judicium egressæ, priscæ sedulitatis inventione nostram adæta-tem pervenit, in differendi subtilita-tem, naturæ evolvendæ obscuritatem, & vitæ beatè degendæ amoenitatem, prisci difpescuernnt. Nec inconcin-na
units.tr: Whatever of human knowledge has come down to our age, rising out of the lowest bench of judgment, by the invention of ancient diligence, the ancients distinguished into three parts: the subtlety of disputation, the obscurity of unfolding nature, and the pleasantness of living a life happily.

units.tr: Not without grace, they built into the domain of philosophy a pleasant garden of playful wit, fenced in by a method of speaking and reasoning, to be viewed with dense and variegated rows of trees, and rich in an abundant yield of fruits sweet to taste. We, fit to gather the vintage of our time, and at the same time reminded of the province committed to us, will fix our contemplation on one part of the last sight. Whoever of you have been admitted to this garden, for the purpose of directing discourse with reason, have fed your eyes on the orderly series of neatly described trees, and your not dishonourable desire of mind, come with me to pluck the fruits. So that this may happen without disgust, I will teach in this little dissertation by what way and under what guide the fruit of these trees is attained. While I run through this with a brief compass, unfolded plainly and not amplified with oratorical circuit, I most humbly ask you to grant me this labour for the small moment of time that flows by. All things that are now enclosed and confined by the bars of art were once wandering and scattered.

units.la: Non loquendi hominibus ratio, non differendi defuit, non involutæ te- gumento suo naturæ denudatio. Ve- rum sermonis, ratiocinationis, con- templationis membratim congesta præcepta defuerunt, Sic ptifcis ante Socratis familiam mortalibus non de suæ administrandæ reipublicæ, & exul- tantium supra rationem affectuum compescendorum meditatio: coaɗta in membrorum compaginem, & quadam ordinis concinnitate consarcinata, mo- rum descriptio defuit. Nunc propriori numinis aspectu, & sagaciori temporum indagine, eo quæsita resex- crevit, ut pauciad fastigium scientiæ rum contingendum apices abesse vide- antur. Sed nec in compendiorum
units.tr: Men did not lack a method of speaking, nor of discoursing; nor was nature, stripped of its enveloping covering, lacking. But precepts of speech, of reasoning and of contemplation, gathered limb by limb, were lacking. So before the school of Socrates, mortals had no meditation on how to administer their commonwealth, nor on restraining the passions that exult beyond reason. A description of morals, brought together into a joined body and patched together with a certain neatness of order, was lacking. Now, by a nearer view of the divine power and a keener investigation of the times, the things that were sought have been so sifted out that only a few steps seem to remain before one reaches the summit of knowledge.

units.tr: But civil principles do not linger in the prisons of compendia, unless they are led out into open space. As formerly there was labour in dispersing the parts, so now there is anxious superstition in binding them together. There are two things which bring forth from a mind well informed by nature the little sparks of prudence hidden in the soul: practice and meditation. Practice opens up in the broad field of the world, through the tasting of government, the careful observation of peoples and states, and the view of court and affairs. Meditation is nourished by the attentive hearing of men who excel in this kind of learning, and by frequent reading of the writers of ancient and more recent times. We do not force practice into precepts; we leave the attention of the listeners to their own judgment. What is to be read, and with what estimate, I will indicate with a finger pointed at the source. So that I may proceed along this winding course without a wandering step, I will divide every kind of writer separately by ages, by kinds of learning, by sects and by nations.

units.tr: In the first rank I consider either antiquity, or the middle age, or the memory of our own time and of our fathers. Among the kinds of learning, I place the teachers of wisdom in the front line, support the poets and orators in the middle, and close the rear with the historians I consult. Among the sects the most noble are the Stoics, Peripatetics, Academics and Epicureans; among the nations the ancient Greeks and Romans; nor are the Germans, French, English, Spanish, Venetians and Etruscans to be despised in this age. So that I may begin, as it were, from the egg, I will set out the ages, names, sects and nations. Those who professed something above the common run, by writing or by speech, to whom modesty gave the name of philosophers, are hardly to be found in our census before the Socratic house, except for certain sayings of PYTHAGORAS and of a few of those called the SEVEN. From SOCRATES, who committed nothing to writing himself, nor asserted anything certain by voice, as from the ridges of the Alps, divergences of doctrine arose just as those of rivers do.

units.tr: The jests of Socrates and his sharp sayings against the sophists were taken up chiefly by two from his flock: Plato and Xenophon. Plato is loftier than Xenophon, more florid, and more expansive, with the reins loosed. Xenophon is more restrained than Plato, and more compact, cut short of the long circuit of preambles. Plato, enriching the discourse of Socrates with the gift of words, poured it out as at table or in circles, and gradually creeps into the minds of his readers; with the sweetness of his speech and the unexpected sting of his conclusions, he carries them off to admiration of virtue. In enacting laws, and in shaping the commonwealth from tender years, he marked out both many things that would profit when scattered, and some that depart from the customs of men, indeed from the honesty of life. From him, through Xenocrates, derived the ACADEMICS, of ambiguous debate and suspended judgment, who embraced with the greatest fondness what was slightest in Socrates: to oppose everyone's opinion. Since they were born only to overturn men's conceptions, and contribute little weight to the solid foundation of a happy life, and since they display the show of ingenious chatter, the PERIPATETICS (named, in my judgment, not so much from walking about as from the discourse of the mind on both sides) follow Aristotle, the author of the sect, and his successor Theophrastus of honeyed eloquence. I do not know by what right or wrong Epiphanius confuses them with the Pythagoreans. ARISTOTLE, another light rising out of the darkness of Macedonia, first constrained Plato's wandering licence in disputing by fixed precepts and a stricter method of teaching. He, although wholly given over to dialectical acuteness and physical subtlety, and delighted by a bare treatise of the arts, nevertheless did not omit those things which conduce to living well and to governing the state.

units.tr: Yet he did not neglect the things that serve private life and the governing of the state. His Nicomachean Ethics, written with a pleasing elegance, is a set of ten books; next in order, and in some parts earlier, come the Eudemian books in seven parts; then the little gem-like treatise on defining virtues and vices. These attest that the lion can be known by its claw. The so-called Magna Moralia, which do not match the greatness of their name, in my judgment do not have the same worth. Either they fell from his feeble old age, or they palmed off on the unwary some ape of Aristotle, to be embraced as Juno in place of a cloud. On governing the household, parents and spouses, and on enriching oneself with added wealth, the Economics ran in a two-horse chariot, not very loosely girded. The Science of Civil Government is higher than both and, explaining itself more widely, is more exposed to the shifts of changing times.

units.la: magis obnoxiam, Civilis regiminis scientiam, octo, quae quidem ad nos pervenerint, voluminibus complexus æternitati consecravit. Tum ipso Ni-comachiorum vestibulo, Imperio ei in omnes disciplinas assignato, Ethicam ut partem toti, aut ut membrum inferi-us capiti subjecit. Magnam debemus tanto autori gratiam, qui tanta ingenii sagacitate, tanta commentandi folertia, fundamenta nobilissimæ doctrinæ, & quandam operis ad culmen educendi delineationem, primus inventam tra-didit. Quod ad robustiorem exstru-ctionem ædificii contignationem, si quintum librum arcanorum Imperii premendi plenum excipias, pauca quæ hujus ævi naso fatis faciant deprehendas. Sunt & in RHETORICIS ejus quædam civi-tatis regendæ monita; & de affectu-um ebullientium tristi vel exultanti ge-nio, uberiora etiam quàm in Moralibus, propria eorum fede, ibi feruntur.
units.tr: This he comprised in eight volumes, which have reached us, and consecrated to eternity. Then, at the very threshold of the Nicomachean books, assigning to it dominion over all the disciplines, he placed Ethics beneath it as a part of the whole, or as a lower member subject to the head. We owe great gratitude to so great an author, who with such keenness of mind and such skill in commentary first handed down the foundations of this most noble doctrine, and a sketch for raising the work to its summit. For the sturdier construction of the building, if you except the fifth book, which is full of secrets for holding down an empire, you will find few things that satisfy the taste of this age. There are also in his Rhetoric some admonitions on governing the state, and about the sorrowful or exultant disposition of agitated emotions; these are offered more fully there, in their proper seat, than in the Moralia.

units.la: In moribus ad vivum depingendis & foeditate criminum quafrin speculo o-ftendenda, felicis est ingenuitatis, nomè: ab eloquentia divina sortitus, THEO-PHRASTUS: opusculo inprimis quod CHARACTERUM nomine a remonstranda intignivit. Animo sa STOICORUM; & sa- stidita humo ccelum tentans natio, quā- tum virtutis commendatione sibi auto- ritatis conciunavit, tantum ariditate di- ctionis; & vano in refería verborum aucupio detraxit.
units.tr: In portraying manners to the life and showing the foulness of crimes as in a mirror, the name of a happy nobility of genius was won from divine eloquence by THEOPHRASTUS, chiefly through the little work that made him famous under the title of Characters. The Stoics, a sect that, with a lofty spirit, disdained the earth and tried to reach heaven, won as much authority for themselves by commending virtue as they lost through the dryness of their style and their vain hunting after far-fetched words.

units.tr: But the masters of Roman eloquence, TULLY, I mean, and SENECA, rescued them from oblivion, to the great benefit of the young. Yet in Seneca, a writer of lofty gravity, there are some things, arrogantly disparaging pride and the empire of God, or commending violent hands, which must be avoided as shoals to a sailor. Somewhat more humble, and mindful of his servile fortune, EPICTETUS, born in an age already sinking into crudeness, smells in his poverty of speech and his strangeness of maxims of the decay and old age of the ancient Porch.

units.tr: Certainly Aristotle generously grants that a certain pleasure comes with the fellowship of the blessed life; and the Portuenses themselves, venerable for the gravity of their brow, when they come from words to deeds, do not banish every charm of a pleasant life from the company of a stricter life. The pleasures of the mind were to be separated from those of the body; and among the bodily pleasures, those that are necessary, those honestly permitted rather than forbidden, and those that are wholesome were to be distinguished from those that are harmful. Not that human blessedness is placed in these at a higher level, but so that they do not disdain the place of attendants and handmaids. I observe that Epicurus was an object of admiration to his own people, because no philosopher laboured more diligently than he to raise man above fear and above desire, secure against every onslaught of fortune. units.tr: HIEROCLES, MAXIMUS OF TYRE, IAMBLICHUS, MUSONIUS; and, more favourable to Aristotle, PORPHYRY and SIMPLICIUS, who flourished in the middle age. I hesitate in judgment whether to count PLUTARCH of Chaeronea among the band of historians, or to enrol him in the flock of philosophers, the eternal herald of unfeigned virtue and the incorruptible sponsor of historical truth. It is not worth the effort to enumerate all in this census, nor is there room in the span of time allotted to me. In the Roman Latin arena, now retired, the palm for professing wisdom is won by BOETHIUS alone. Soon, as subtlety in disputing increased and the elegance of speech declined, a new kind of doctrine emerged, mingled from Aristotle and the Fathers of Christian theology, or rather entangling Aristotle and the Fathers in each other's explanations.

units.tr: I do not detract from the diligence of PETER LOMBARD in gathering sentences; I do not call back to censure the profound acumen of THOMAS AQUINAS; I do not accuse SCOTUS of dullness, nor of idleness in tying and untying knots. I live with virtues and unadulterated juice, though peoples are restrained by the rein of empire; how the subtle crowd of the Schoolmen greatly helps us, I do not perceive. In that age too, brought back on the stage of the academy with a purer file of judgment, the elegance of polished speech began; nor was there almost anyone of improved talent who, in depicting morals, did not follow Aristotle's footsteps, roughened with Tullian flowers of words. In politics, however, licence began to venture more boldly and not to keep within the barriers prescribed by Peripatetic narrowness. Nor should you expect from me here praise or censure of individuals who have dared something in that kind of writing; for that would seem burdensome through its length and invidious through the rashness of judgment. I shall lead through the nations in general, not through houses and persons, and that by leaps and steps. The GERMANS seek eternal fame chiefly through methodical elegance and the wide cultivation of public law. The DUTCH, an ancient offspring of the Germans, and whoever among the Scandinavians break through the northern darkness with the rays of judgment, search out the antiquity of history. The ENGLISH, as in the contemplation of nature, so in forming morals and the right of command, scorning the path of their elders, chase the rumour of ingenious boldness from the sharpness of new invention. The FRENCH, after Bodin and Toulouse, men of learning not to be despised, have slipped into the courtly delights of vernacular flattery, and are excessive in praising their own kings or purple-clad men, and in vilifying the followers of the Austrian house

No other nation has investigated more penetratingly what they call Reason of State, or explained it more fully and made it known in the vernacular to ears capable of the mystery. The SPANIARDS, lest they be thought to have been ignominiously passed over, strive to spread their Secret of State, publishing it by deeds as much as by writings. In the Sarmatian language, some sharp things written about the king and the state of the kingdom are eagerly read, but, as I judged at the time, they had already been chewed over by the Italians, the satellites of the King of Poland. I come to the middle storey of the civil and moral structure, elegantly inlaid with the planks of the poets. Nor should anyone frown at our combining fictions with truth, and wit with dignity. units.tr: by nature truth conquers imitation, yet, given human nature, imitation sometimes has more power than truth to move the emotions. Nor should every mark of fictitious wantonness be cast upon everything that circulates in the wide estate of the chaste poets, nor should a pleasantness that presents itself obstruct a hidden use. Poetry is not inappropriately the mark of a flowing talent, whose power of penetration both bends the minds of unrefined people by the sweetness of its measured rhythm, and strikes the mind more forcefully with a sentence enclosed in numbers, and whose song, pleasantly striking the imagination, is carried about and held longer in memory by its images. Nor have we reason to regret the metrical turning of words, as if it were a cheapness that lowers them beneath the gravity of stricter teaching. For if we look at the lot of teaching meant to be committed to memory, all of it will lodge on the estate of the poets. No state of any known nation, except Plato's imaginary one, has ever dismissed poetry from its number, without at the same time banishing from its borders every profession of wisdom. But lest we pluck deadly aconite instead of medicine, or pick poison for a panacea, I advise that not just any poets are to be read indiscriminately, nor that any passages from any sources are to be gathered into the store.

units.la: MUSÆI quæ circum feruntur opuscula, horridam antiquitatem com-to stylo non sapiunt: ut nec decantati priscis poëtis ORPHEI: quorum il-le amoris violentiam culta diͤione producit; hic castigata phrafi purio-rum de Deo mysteriorum adyta reclu-dit.
units.tr: MUSAEUS' little works that circulate under his name do not smell of rough antiquity in their polished style; nor do those of the famous ORPHEUS, among the ancient poets: the one produces the violence of love in refined verse, the other, in chastened phrase, opens the sanctuaries of the purer mysteries about God.

Et quamvis Ho- merici genii sublimitatem nec argu- mento nec dictione assequatur : sen- tentiarum nimbo effuso, cum poëta- rum aquila certaverit. THEOGNI- TUS innocentem pastorum vitam, ambitione procul & aviditate degen- tem, nec suas aut alienas fortunas metu & spe versantem, grata pangendi carminis dulcedine cantillat. PHOCYLIDES, & PYTHAGORÆab auro denominatum carmen, nec non THEOGNIS & SOLONIS quæ-dam, & aliorum gnomas sefantium, in adolescentum formandis moribus opellam impendunt. Quorum PHOCYLLIDES à Christianisimi puritate haud longe abest: PYTHAGO-RAS ad fabulosas ineptias delabitur. Quos hactenus recensui, præcipiti transfitu lustratos, partim EPICO-RUM & HEROICORUM, partim ELEGIACORUM nomine, à pari pedum aut dispari mensura. sura, censentur. LYRICORUM caput PINDARUS, audaci di- thyramborum impetu procurrens, sententiarum jaculatu parcus, ludicras magnatum victorias ad fastidium de- prædicat, ANACREON protervæ venustratis felix Magister; ut & puel- larum amoribus insana SAPPHO, & omnes in eo ingenii valetudinario defixi, ad severiorem palæstræ confess- fumnon temere admittuntur. ætna- signa Comœdia bustis ereptus A.R.I- STOPHANES, à puritate di- ctionis Atticæ laudem adeptus, impu- so sensu verborum delestum contami- navit. units.tr: sharpness; which, with peace to those preoccupied by prejudice, abounds. Yet with fictitious examples, or monstrously exaggerated ones, and by a certain rapture of poetic frenzy, he kindles minds to virtue, warlike in the Iliad or peaceful in the Odyssey. HESIOD, in the Theogony, tediously and absurdly thrusts upon us gods who are born and grow old; in the Shield of Hercules he strives for grand eloquence beyond his powers; in the Works and Days he shapes the head of the household with domestic examples and youth with moral lessons, with a certain artless simplicity. And although he does not attain the sublimity of Homer's genius either in subject or in diction, with a pouring cloud of sentences he has competed with the eagle of the poets. THEOGNIS, in a pleasing sweetness of song, sings of the innocent life of shepherds, living far from ambition and greed, not troubled by fear and hope about their own or others' fortunes. PHOCYLIDES, and the Golden Poem named after Pythagoras, as well as some of Theognis and Solon, and the maxims of others speaking in gnomes, devote their little work to forming the morals of young people. Of these, Phocylides is not far from the purity of Christianity; Pythagoras slides into fabulous absurdities. In shaping his Cyrnus for virtue, Theognis admits both much idle and cold matter and, as if granted to the more youthful age of adolescence, a certain wantonness. CALLIMACHUS, equal to Theognis in his kind of verse and superior in charm, sprinkles a market of sentences with the open rouge of lascivious Venus. These I have reviewed, passing over them hastily, are counted partly under the name of EPIC and HEROIC, partly under ELEGIAC, from equal or unequal measure of feet. PINDAR, the head of the LYRIC poets, rushing forward with the bold impetus of dithyrambs, sparing in the hurling of sentences, extols to the point of tedium the playful victories of the great. ANACREON, a happy master of wanton charm, and SAPPHO, mad with love for girls, and all who are fixed in that sickly genius, are not rashly admitted to the stricter wrestling-ground. ARISTOPHANES, rescued from the tombs of comedy, won praise for the purity of Attic diction, but polluted his meaning with obscene sense of words. Although Chrysostom, the great bishop among the holy men, took delight in him, the same guard of a chaste mind is not kept by all. Of MENANDER and of more recent comedy, which is more modest in speech, few pieces, broken and worn, have come down to us, chiefly thanks to the gathering of STOBAEUS.

AESCHYLUS is sublime, to be held in esteem by the rulers of states on account of the height of his spirit and genius. EURIPIDES, dragging the buskin low, though he portrays the fortunes of kings wretchedly, reminds common life of its frailty, scorning the plebeian. From the old rags of sentences of NAEVIUS, PACUVIUS, CAECILIUS and ACCIUS, PLAUTUS, polished in the flow of Roman speech, has been stitched together as a support for this age for shaping morals and governing the state: he delights the theatre, stirring up laughter from young people and seeking applause, while a certain crop of sentences is overwhelmed by the playful salt of wit. Some formulas of the ancient Roman forum and traces of old law, together with the bare propriety of Latin, he draws not unsuitably from the wreckage of their gaps. TERENCE, more polished in phrase and chaster in the sense conveyed, corrects, from domestic life, the lapses that lead toward civil conduct: youthful luxury of adolescents, the crafty fraud of slaves, the credulous ease of old men, which are easily led astray.

VIRGIL, MARO, having gained by the common suffrage of nations the dictatorship among the poets, in the pastoral decade of his ECLOGUES consults pleasure more than use, and the seasoning of learning more than profit, unless one twists it out through violent allegories. Less delightful, the GEORGICS, with their rustic consolations of life, presents a wonderful cultivation of rough material by a diligent genius, with maxims inserted like emblems. But the work of the AENEID, not recalled to the anvil on a grand scale, extols the civil and military virtue of the Prince, and the steadfastness of Aeneas in adversity, feigned as a shadow of truth, and moderation in prosperity. I would think the Venusian poet HORACE, who sells himself not so much by Venus as by the height of his sentences, should be pruned of a few Odes and a good part of the Satires, and then imprinted on the mind and memory of learners. He is profound in the Odes, middling in the Satires, and eloquent beyond the condition of human genius in the Epistles. A. TIBULLUS, flowing gently like a river through pleasant meadows, commends a life removed from cares, to be lived far from avarice and envy. CORNELIUS GALLUS, grave in his trifles, amid the gasping laments of mad love, eloquently bewails the burden of advancing age and the threats of imminent death. PROPERTIUS, resonant in the Callimachean Muse, discourses with sonorous gravity on the power of love and its giddy misery, on the immortality of fame won by genius, on the necessity of death which no one can escape, on restraining the greed for gold, and on the forces to be weighed in business. The volumes of the Metamorphoses, which seem to have been snatched from the anvil and still await the final polish, are drawn out with a talent that surpasses the ease of the Greeks, with an artful connection of the fabulous matters arranged in sequence; many things serve to commend the divine power, many to praise the virtues, and they instruct. The Heroides, the Epistles and the replies to them, the modulations of the Sirens' song that kill, to be heard with the desires bound fast, and the Remedia Amoris and the remedy for the wound of desire would have had no place, had the mind not been wounded beforehand by the poisoned darts of the Amores and the Ars amatoria. The tragedy of L. Annaeus Seneca, if any part of poetic invention, rich in weighty maxims and with a spirit raised above the power of fortune, comes forward on the stage in the toga; yet there is in it something we must guard against: the elation of mind, the rash defiance of fate, and the reckless eagerness to bring on death headlong. Persius and Juvenal, as the chief writers of satire, are handled by the hands of young people on account of their long-standing reputation. For my part I do not acknowledge Persius as a craftsman of solid learning, his obscurity being caused more by ignorance of things than by depth of thought; I find Juvenal biting without any salt of wit, too open in exposing the monstrous foulness of vices to the eyes, yet not barren of maxims. Lucan, keeping little measure in his words and closer to historical truth, is to be scrutinized in his military and civil matters, not without regret, as he stumbles in his stride and advances with an uncertain step. units.tr: Demosthenes' style is more vigorous and manly, suited to rousing minds for war; Isocrates' is gentler in both life and speech, and better fitted to keeping people at peace. Among the Roman masters of eloquence, besides Tullius and Seneca already mentioned, there are Quintilian, Fabius, and Marcus Seneca, who train students in the schoolroom arena. As for Pliny's Panegyric on Trajan, I think it loses a great deal of its value. Nor should the orators of our own age be wholly neglected when they handle public affairs skilfully. As for the poets of this age and the last, I refrain from comment. Those who have proved worthy of the name offer more sweetness to delight the reader than strength to teach him. Otherwise, unless they bear the stamp of antiquity, they supply neither the grace of beauty nor the sinews of the limbs.

units.tr: But after the armed line of the philosophers, and after the auxiliary forces of poets and orators, the thundering legion of historians must at last be brought forward. To reduce history to art and precepts was a necessity; to sprinkle it with poetic ornament, a matter of delight; to lay it on the foundation of history, a matter of solidity. Yet not all who have written of the counsels of senators or the deeds of commanders are to be measured with the same rod of dignity or indignity. Some supply planks for building the ship of the commonwealth; others contribute scraps, tow and pitch. Herodotus, fortunate above the rest in the amplitude of his material, will show by examples how great kingdoms were overthrown by the foolish confidence of power, and how small peoples of the poor, with weak but united strength, were raised up by the providence of wise counsel and by courage conspiring for vengeance.

units.tr: Thucydides, by his dignified but unaffected style, and by his almost weighing of individual words in the balance of his sentences, and by his deep probing of hidden counsels, lends authority to the Greek nation. Xenophon, sweeter in diction but weaker in the sinews of his matter, in his Greek History and in the Expedition of Cyrus and the return of the Greeks from Persia, revealed to his countrymen the feebleness of the Persian kingdom's power and the nakedness of its side, now already unnerved. In the other kinds of writing he is more tenacious of truth; in his portrait of Cyrus, which is shaped to an image of virtue, he is more instructive in political discipline. Polybius, besides the shrewdness of a Greek mind, was sharpened by his experience of the Roman war against the Carthaginians and by his intimacy with Scipio, the greatest of the Roman commanders. I commend Dionysius of Halicarnassus for bringing to light the moments of Roman antiquity hidden in darkness, Diodorus Siculus for the connection of times and nations with the Roman empire, and Appian for his clear exposition of the penetration of warfare.

units.tr: Dio, Zosimus, Herodian, Xiphilinus, and others, if any have recorded the deeds and events of the Augusti, I will not waste my time on work that is not to be despised. Nor is Zonaras to be overlooked, who has followed the events from the creation of the world down to the Emperor Alexius in a modest exposition. After him comes Nicetas Choniates, who, though often clumsy in the gesturing of an extravagant style, has either omitted or patched together the deeds of degenerate Greece in a not useless thread of history. Nicephorus Gregoras, the hyperaspistes of this man, shining out from the ruins, raised up the Byzantine empire with laborious but not entirely successful effort. When it was again more grievously shaken by the Bulgarians and stripped of all dignity by the Turks, Chalcocondylas, a citizen of Athens, with an elegant pen, completes the account of the origin, progress and warlike virtue of the Turks, which is to be recorded. Ecclesiastical history writers contribute less to civil administration, yet they are by no means to be neglected by a politician, at least because of the context of their time. If it does not displease, let me summon to the account some of the ancient bishops of theology and the divine orators of the sacred mystery: Basil with the lofty weight of his sentences, Nazianzen with the ease of his eloquence, John Chrysostom with his detection of vices that penetrates the minds of his hearers, and Clement of Alexandria, who will offer learning seasoned with a taste of antiquity. Synesius, though unequal in other respects to the lofty mind of Chrysostom and Basil, also rises to describe the reins of government. Athanasius and Theodoret, lifted above the clouds by the sublimity of heavenly wisdom, do not allow themselves to descend to the censure of morals or to the care of earthly empires. But from minds of such a kind, having searched things higher than those of this life, I turn the helm of my discourse by an oblique turn to the writers of civil and military affairs.

units.tr: The Romans, yielding to the Greeks the subtlety of philosophizing, and not contending too much for the applause of the theatre in poetry, have come close to surpassing them in the majesty of writing history. For just as they excelled in the constant practice of ruling, in greatness of spirit and military fortune, and in unconquered steadiness amid uncertainties, so too, with a style matching the greatness of their spirit and skill in writing from long practice with affairs, they approached the matters to be pursued. These themselves, advancing with a great interval between them in talent, are not to be brought forth with equal esteem, nor indiscriminately at all times. Before the battle-line of robust virtue run forward the skirmishers, easy in words and sense, the writers of epitomes. Among them, Justin, who followed the vicissitudes of peoples from the empire of the Assyrians founded by Ninus down to his own time, or that of Pompeius Trogus, which he compiled by compressing it into narrow limits; Aemilius Probus, who followed the footsteps of Cornelius Nepos in describing the lives of great commanders among Greeks and Romans. Having emerged from these as recruits, Florus and Velleius Paterculus bind themselves to recommend themselves by the richer juice of weightier words and sentiments, describing the cradle, growth, manhood and aging of the Roman empire. Caesar and Curtius, nearer to the veteran army of writers, unfold great wars that are great undertakings for great commanders. Curtius is more ready with the rounded throw of sentences; Caesar is more skilful in the construction of war and in shrewd contrivances, in building them up and in depicting them to the life. Valerius Maximus, with a grandiloquence not without a touch of coldness, if he had aimed at the purity of a clear style, might have greatly delighted his readers by arranging examples of virtue in a neat method. To these, when they have been unrolled, and before the systematic tradition of politics, with precepts compacted into an art, let Titus Livy be cultivated with more attentive care, as the eternal glory of the city of Padua; yielding perhaps to others in gentleness of words, but more lofty in matter and variety of events.

units.tr: Let Crispus Sallust suffice, who has been turned into juice and marrow, burning with an ardent desire to know and to discuss, with a spirit that is warm in its terse brevity, and with a manly virtue breathing, almost word by word, an ancient restraint. Cornelius Tacitus, the greatest of the veteran writers of the army, always to be spoken of with care, the most skilled investigator of the courts and of the army, shall be unrolled in the last place, but not with the last care. To these we add Suetonius Tranquillus, as a kind of commentator, not rising to the majesty of deciding for an emperor. What crowd of writers follows after the Emperor Trajan breathes in style the languor of an empire failing in virtue. Because of the continuity of history, and for reconciling them with the Greeks, we shall run through them briefly, spending a little more time in Ammianus. Of those who wrote in the middle ages of time, or as our own age was drawing near, in a language foreign to both Greeks and Romans, Commines is celebrated for his talkative fame. Nor would I detract from his judgment, which was formed by experience of war and of the court. Yet if I compare him with any of the ancients, I find him not sufficiently polished in Gallic diction for the ears of these times,

units.tr: I find no one who is sparing in putting forward opinions about the commonwealth yet plebeian in ready speech. Nearer to the palm of antiquity, Guicciardini in Tuscan and Pierre Matthieu in French would have come, had not the coldness of his digressions and the youthful flattery of his own people held back the one, and the other. More worthy of the threshold of antiquity is the historian of Belgian affairs, the Tuscan Bentivoglio; and if we must stand by popular rather than my own judgement, Vittorio Siri. Nor should those who could commit the deeds of their own age to Latin prose be passed over: Sleidan for the Rhine and Germany, de Thou for the Seine and the French, and Famiano Strada for the Tiber and the renewed Eternal City. Whether for the candour of their judgement, their insight into the secrets of kings and peoples, or their knowledge of public law, they are unworthy of the diligence of the ancients, and let them be mown down by the sickle of a scornful judgement. If anything is to be yielded also to the early teachers of the Latin Church: Augustine, set aside for the subtlety of his disputations, will drip with the fine things Ambrose says about the duties of human life, the admirable things Jerome says, the sinewy things Cyprian says, and Lactantius, flowing with abundance. Tertullian, attacking the profane nations, and together with him Arnobius, will stir up the outworn rites of antiquity, which a statesman should not disdain.

Aeter-nam universi mentem, ante mundum & fine mundi concretione existentem, extre; mapagina venetor, mihi ut ad docendi metam, indcfeffo cursu emetiendam, fer; monis vires; nobili studiosorum juventu; tiad me assiduè, & non poeniteando cum fructu, audiendum generosos motus in-spiret. Tum omnes docendi & discendi conatus ad supremam actionum omnium metam, nominis divini nunc temporariam post sempiternam celebrationem, ipsa deducat.
units.tr: If I were to enlarge on how much knowledge of Attic, Roman and feudal law will be needed by the future practitioner, and, in certain knotty cases, of canon law; or how much knowledge of Holy Scripture must be sought, both for regulating life by the plumb-line of the divine will and for settling controversies of faith by public authority, the day would fail me in my speech, and both my powers of utterance and the patience of my hearers would give out. So I shall not stretch out the orbit of my discourse so much as indulge my eagerness to speak, since I have set this limit to my course. On the last page I seek the eternal mind of the universe, which existed before the world and will exist at its dissolution. May it give me strength of speech, to be traversed with a tireless course to the goal of teaching; and may it inspire the noble youth of the students to hear me constantly and with profit, and without regret. Then may it itself lead all the efforts of teaching and learning to the supreme goal of all actions, the celebration of the divine name, now for a time, and afterwards for eternity.
